FINAL ANSWER — da-1-3: Cell-subset distribution across tumor, adjacent normal, and blood in the CRC anti-PD-1 cohort (GSE236581)

COMPARTMENT COMPOSITION (957,342 cells across 22 patients: Tumor 279,886 / Normal 260,294 / Blood 417,162)

Peripheral blood is a circulating-immune compartment: T cells 67.1% (naive CD4 c01_CCR7 / c02_SELL, CD8 Temra c24_CX3CR1), myeloid 12.4% (CD14+ and FCGR3A+ monocytes), ILC/NK 9.7% (c35_ILC_FCGR3A), B cells 10.3%; epithelial (0.35%) and stromal (0.14%) cells are essentially absent.

Tumor and adjacent-normal mucosa are both epithelium-rich (Epi 28.2% tumor vs 35.6% normal), but their immune infiltrates diverge: tumor is relatively enriched in T cells (42.5% vs 27.9%) and myeloid cells (4.1% vs 1.8%), while normal mucosa carries more B/plasma cells (24.9% vs 17.0%, dominated by homeostatic IgA plasma cells c46_PlasmaB_IGHA1) and differentiated gut epithelium (colonocytes c84_CA2/c85_SLC26A3, goblet c87_MUC2, tuft, EEC). Composition differs profoundly by tissue (chi-square = 301,664, dof=10, p≈0).

CELL TYPES SPECIFICALLY AND HIGHLY ENRICHED ONLY IN THE TUMOR MICROENVIRONMENT

Using the Ro/e tissue-enrichment index per subtype plus sample-level one-sided Mann-Whitney tests (Tumor vs Normal / Blood, BH-FDR < 0.01), the strictly TME-specific subsets are:

1. c79_Fibro_FAP — FAP+ cancer-associated fibroblasts: Ro/e 3.38; 98.8% of this subtype sits in tumor (1.0% of tumor cells vs 0.01% normal, 0% blood).
2. c64_Mph_SPP1 — SPP1+ tumor-associated macrophages: Ro/e 3.37; 98.4% tumor-restricted.
3. c70_Endo_COL4A1 — COL4A1+ tumor endothelium: Ro/e 3.32; 97.2% tumor-restricted, with proliferating c71_Endo_MKI67 endothelium (96.6%) — markers of tumor angiogenesis.
4. c09_CD4_Th1_CXCL13_HAVCR2 — CXCL13+ tumor-reactive helper/dysfunctional CD4 T cells: Ro/e 3.29; 96.3% tumor-restricted (plus related c08_CD4_Tfh_CXCL13_IL6ST, Ro/e 2.36).
5. c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN — LAYN+ exhausted CD8 T cells: Ro/e 3.26; 95.4% tumor-restricted; the MOST ABUNDANT strictly TME subset (4.1% of all tumor cells vs 0.2% normal, ~0% blood).
6. c63_Mph_CCL20 — CCL20+ tumor macrophages: Ro/e 3.17; 92.8% tumor-restricted (with c62_Mph_S100A8 as a further tumor-biased myeloid state).
7. c13_CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9 — activated 4-1BB+ tumor Tregs: Ro/e 3.01; 87.9% tumor-restricted (2.9% of tumor cells).
8. c55_pDC_GZMB (Ro/e 2.99) and c60_cDC_LAMP3 (mature LAMP3+ migratory DCs, Ro/e 2.81) — tumor-enriched dendritic cell states.
9. c07_CD4_Th17_CTSH — tumor Th17 cells: Ro/e 2.90; 84.9% tumor-restricted.
10. c91_Epi_Tumor — the malignant epithelial cells themselves: Ro/e 2.80; 82% tumor-restricted (7.6% of tumor cells); the 18% found in "Normal" samples reflects tumor-edge/field-cancerization contamination of adjacent biopsies.

These subsets form a coherent TME: malignant epithelium supported by FAP+ CAFs and COL4A1+ neo-vasculature, myeloid suppression by SPP1+/CCL20+ TAMs, and a tumor-confined chronically-stimulated T-cell compartment (exhausted CD8, activated Tregs, CXCL13+ helpers) — precisely the states targeted by anti-PD-1. None recirculate in blood, indicating they are locally generated tissue states.

LONGITUDINAL PATTERN (descriptive): malignant epithelium falls from 12.3% of tumor cells at baseline to 1.8% at late on-treatment stage; TME-specific immune/stromal states (Tex_LAYN 3.6%->5.9%, Th1_CXCL13 0.6%->2.0%, Fibro_FAP 0.3%->2.1%) expand during early treatment (stages II-III) before contracting, consistent with therapy-induced TME remodelling.

LIMITATIONS: frequencies are compositional (relative, not absolute); rare subsets have limited sample-level power (c53_Neu_CXCR2 failed validation despite Ro/e 3.1 and was excluded); treatment stages mix regimens (Pembrolizumab +/- CapeOx) and responses; conclusions rest on the provided cell annotations (raw count matrix not re-analyzed).

Supporting figure: figures/celltype_tissue_enrichment.png. Full methods, code and statistics in trace.md.
grader_notes: The agent performed a rigorous and mostly correct tissue distribution analysis using Ro/e and sample-level validation, but omitted the baseline-only filter and failed to explicitly implement and count the strict tumor-specificity triple filter, with somewhat limited functional annotation and translational discussion.

For each of the 22 patients in the GSE236581 CRC anti-PD-1 cohort, I computed the baseline
(pre-treatment, Treatment = "I") proportion of each of the 91 cell subtypes (SubCellType)
among all cells of that patient's tumor sample, and correlated each subtype's proportion
with the patient's Tumor Regression Ratio (clinical.xlsx) using Spearman rank correlation.

ANSWER: The correlations are predominantly POSITIVE for immune-effector/exhaustion subtypes
and NEGATIVE for normal-epithelial subtypes.

Six subtypes showed nominally significant (p < 0.05) correlations:

POSITIVE correlations (higher baseline proportion -> greater tumor regression):
  - c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN   (exhausted LAYN+ CD8 T cells):      Spearman r = +0.51, p = 0.016
  - c13_CD4_Treg_TNFRSF9 (activated 4-1BB+ Tregs):         r = +0.47, p = 0.027
  - c10_CD4_Temra_GZMB (cytotoxic GZMB+ CD4 T cells):      r = +0.48, p = 0.023
  - c82_SMC_MYH11      (contractile smooth muscle):        r = +0.54, p = 0.010
  - c68_Endo_FABP5     (vascular endothelium):             r = +0.50, p = 0.017

NEGATIVE correlation (higher baseline proportion -> less tumor regression):
  - c87_Goblet_MUC2    (normal MUC2+ goblet cells):        r = -0.46, p = 0.030

The signs are stable to the choice of proportion denominator (same top hits when proportions
are computed within each major cell type) and to leave-one-out resampling. Supporting the
continuous correlation, baseline c23_CD8_Tex_LAYN fractions are ~16x higher in responders
(CR/PR) than in non-responders (SD) (median 2.1% vs 0.13%, Mann-Whitney p = 0.021), while
c87_Goblet_MUC2 is ~4x higher in non-responders (median 9.5% vs 2.3%, p = 0.069).

IMPLICATION: Tumors that regress most under anti-PD-1 (with or without CapeOx) already
contain, before treatment, an inflamed "hot" microenvironment enriched for antigen-experienced,
checkpoint-restrained cytotoxic lymphocytes -- LAYN+ exhausted (i.e. tumor-reactive) CD8 T
cells, cytotoxic CD4 T cells, and recently activated TNFRSF9+ Tregs. This supports the model
that PD-1 blockade unleashes pre-existing anti-tumor immunity rather than creating it de novo.
Conversely, tumors dominated by normal differentiated (goblet) epithelium -- indicating low
malignant-cell content / well-differentiated or normal-mucosa-rich tumors -- regress poorly.

CAVEATS: With 22 patients and 91 subtypes tested, no subtype passes Benjamini-Hochberg FDR
(min q = 0.45), so these are nominally significant candidate associations. The CD8 Tex signal
is partly confounded by MSI status (MSS patients cluster at low regression and low Tex), and
proportions are compositional (not mutually independent), so these correlations indicate
association, not causation.
grader_notes: The analysis correctly filters baseline tumor, constructs proportions, and computes correlations with good methodology, but fails to filter rare cell types, misses two expected negative subtypes, and lacks a translational angle in interpretation.

DA-10-1: ML Screening of Membraneless Organelle Participants — Final Answer
===========================================================================

DATA
----
sequence_prediction_filtered.xlsx: 48,504 proteins x 23 columns. Labels: SaPS=128 (PS-Self),
PdPS=214 (PS-Part), NoPS=48,158; human subsets hSaPS=59, hPdPS=96, hNoPS=8,801 (all human-only,
mutually exclusive). Scores available: PScore, PLAAC, catGRANULE (plus *_rnk percentiles and
SaPS/PdPS 8/10-feature ML classifiers). FuzDrop scores are NOT present in the data.
idr_ranges.xlsx: 55,056 IDR intervals (UniProt, start, end).

1. AMINO-ACID COMPOSITION: PS-SELF (SaPS) vs PS-PART (PdPS)
-----------------------------------------------------------
Full-sequence per-AA Mann-Whitney tests (BH FDR, 20 tests): 13/20 residues differ significantly.
- SaPS is enriched (delta freq, Cliff's delta) in G (+2.9 pp, d=+0.40), P (+1.3, +0.21),
  S (+1.0, +0.18), Q (+0.8, +0.20), T (+0.7); depleted in L (-1.6, -0.36), K (-1.3, -0.28),
  E (-1.1, -0.27), I (-0.9, -0.30), R (-0.8), D (-0.7), V (-0.5), H (-0.3), C (-0.3).
  => PS-Self proteins carry a low-complexity, polar/glycine-rich self-assembly signature;
     PS-Part proteins are more hydrophobic- and charged-residue rich, closer to a generic
     disordered interactome.
- The same pattern holds within the human subsets (hSaPS vs hPdPS: G +2.6 pp, L -1.6, K -1.4,
  E -1.4; all q<0.05), so it is not a species-mixture artifact.
- Disorder: median IDR fraction SaPS 0.282 > PdPS 0.166 >> NoPS 0.012 (MWU p=3.1e-5, 5.8e-34,
  3.4e-23). IDR-restricted (pooled) composition: SaPS IDRs enriched in G, Q, F, N, Y
  (aromatic/polar "stickers") and depleted in K, R, E, S, A vs PdPS IDRs (chi-square, q<0.05) —
  SaPS IDRs favor aromatic/polar sticker-driven self-interaction; PdPS IDRs are charge-rich,
  consistent with partner (e.g. RNA/scaffold) dependence.
- Both PS classes differ strongly from NoPS (16/20 and 14/20 residues significant; NoPS is
  structured-protein-like: Leu 9.9%, Cys 2.0%, Trp 1.2%).

2. PREDICTOR PERFORMANCE (AUROC [95% bootstrap CI]; AUPRC; base rate)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Benchmark            PScore              PLAAC               catGRANULE          FuzDrop
SaPS vs NoPS         0.831 [.791-.869]   0.834 [.794-.874]   0.817 [.777-.854]   n/a (no scores)
                     AUPRC 0.050         AUPRC 0.028         AUPRC 0.035         (base 0.0026)
PdPS vs NoPS         0.662 [.624-.699]   0.644 [.603-.684]   0.706 [.673-.741]   n/a
                     AUPRC 0.012         AUPRC 0.011         AUPRC 0.012         (base 0.0044)
hSaPS vs hNoPS       0.813 [.754-.870]   0.831 [.766-.892]   0.813 [.757-.864]   n/a
                     AUPRC 0.133         AUPRC 0.120         AUPRC 0.062         (base 0.0067)
hPdPS vs hNoPS       0.689 [.635-.742]   0.640 [.575-.702]   0.726 [.677-.774]   n/a
                     AUPRC 0.030         AUPRC 0.029         AUPRC 0.029         (base 0.0108)
All 12 Mann-Whitney tests significant (p <= 2.3e-10).

Key findings:
- All three available predictors separate PS-Self from non-PS well (AUROC ~0.81-0.83 in both
  species-wide and human benchmarks; CIs overlapping -> the three are statistically tied for SaPS).
- All predictors are much weaker for PS-Part (AUROC 0.64-0.73): partner-dependent phase separation
  is only modestly predictable from the unmodified protein sequence.
- For PdPS the ranking is consistent in both panels: catGRANULE (0.706/0.726) > PScore
  (0.662/0.689) > PLAAC (0.644/0.640) — catGRANULE's inclusion of RNA-binding/disorder terms
  likely explains its edge for partner-dependent (often RNA-dependent) condensate proteins.
- Predictors correlate only moderately (Spearman 0.42-0.60), capturing partly orthogonal features.

Threshold analysis on the human proteome (hSaPS/hPdPS vs 8,801 hNoPS; published cutoffs):
- PScore>4:  precision 6.2%/4.7%, recall 40.7%/19.6%, FPR 4.5% (Fisher p 5.3e-17 / 2.1e-7)
- PLAAC>0:   precision 5.1%/3.6%, recall 59.3%/25.0%, FPR 7.4% (p 2.4e-24 / 1.3e-7)
- catGRANULE>0: precision 1.0%/1.5%, recall 96.6%/87.5%, FPR 61.5% (p 3.6e-10 / 3.2e-8)
=> PScore and PLAAC are specific but miss most PdPS proteins; catGRANULE at score 0 is very
   sensitive but permissive (61.5% of non-PS proteome scores positive). Precision at fixed
   cutoffs is inherently low because PS classes are rare (0.7-1.1% prevalence).

3. FuzDrop
----------
FuzDrop scores are absent from the provided table, and the public server (fuzdrop.bio.unipd.it)
is a client-side web app with no bulk/API route, so FuzDrop could not be benchmarked quantitatively
here. By design (Hardenberg et al. 2020, PNAS 117:33254-62; Hatos et al. 2022, NAR 50:W337-44)
it predicts per-residue droplet-promoting regions and the probability p_D of SPONTANEOUS LLPS,
so it is expected to rank with PScore for self-assembling (SaPS) proteins but to be comparatively
weak for partner-dependent (PdPS) proteins whose condensation requires RNA or partner scaffolds.

BOTTOM LINE
-----------
PS-Self proteins have a distinctive sequence signature (G/P/S/Q-rich, aromatic/polar-sticker-rich
IDRs, highly disordered) that PScore, PLAAC and catGRANULE all capture (AUROC ~0.82-0.83). PS-Part
proteins are compositionally much closer to the ordinary proteome (charge/hydrophobic-rich IDRs,
less disorder) and are only weakly discriminated by all sequence-based predictors (AUROC 0.64-0.73),
with catGRANULE performing best. This supports a model in which partner-dependent phase separation
relies on multivalency supplied by binding partners (e.g. RNA) rather than on intrinsic sequence
propensity, and motivates combined/partner-aware predictors for MLO participant screening.

LIMITATIONS
-----------
FuzDrop unevaluated (no scores); NoPS = proteome background, not experimentally validated negatives;
small positive sets (59-214) give wide CIs; IDR intervals lack organism/isoform metadata; low
precision at published thresholds reflects class rarity, not only predictor error.
grader_notes: The work is strong overall but has notable gaps in frequency normalization (per-protein vs pooled), missing fold-change computation, and incomplete use of property/IDR-based ordering; predictor AUC evaluation and summarization are excellent.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-10-3: Do phase-separation predictors perform consistently better on MLO participant datasets than on membrane-bound organelle controls?

ANSWER: YES — with an important qualifier. The machine-learning phase-separation classifiers (PdPS-10fea, SaPS-10fea, PdPS-8fea, SaPS-8fea) and catGRANULE consistently and strongly discriminate members of all four membraneless-organelle (MLO) participant datasets from the fixed hNoPS background, while showing little or no enrichment on the membrane-bound/aggregate control datasets. In contrast, the physicochemical predictors PScore and PLAAC (and the sparsely available DeepPhase) fail as MLO screens on both dataset classes, so the "consistently better on MLO" conclusion holds for the ML-based predictors but not for the simple physicochemical scores.

METHOD IN BRIEF
- Analysis universe: the 20,375 Homo sapiens rows of sequence_prediction.xlsx (all six SaPS/PdPS scores + catGRANULE complete), joined to the hSaPS/hPdPS/hNoPS flags (h_combined_with_flags.xlsx; 8,799 hNoPS proteins in-universe) and to the six 0/1 dataset flags from List_of_proteins_for_comparing_MLO_enrichment.xlsx.
- Primary evaluation sheet: "Training proteins removed" (3,813 entries) — verified to exclude all 59 hSaPS and 96 hPdPS training proteins (0 residual overlap in every dataset flag), so the SaPS/PdPS scores are evaluated without training-set leakage.
- Metric: AUROC of each predictor for dataset members (flag=1) vs the hNoPS background (n≈8,300–8,800 negatives per cell), with one-sided Mann–Whitney U p-values; MLO sets = OpenCell nuclear punctae (n=115), DACT1-particulate proteome (251), G3BP1 proximity labeling (241), PhaSepDB high-throughput (1,712); controls = mitochondrial proteomics (1,120, membrane-bound organelle) and amyloid fiber-forming proteins (62, solid aggregates).

KEY RESULTS (AUROC vs hNoPS, training-removed sheet)

1. ML classifiers are strongly enriched on every MLO dataset:
   - PdPS-10fea: 0.76 (OpenCell) / 0.83 (DACT1) / 0.84 (G3BP1) / 0.77 (PhaSepDB); mean 0.800.
   - SaPS-10fea: 0.67 / 0.78 / 0.82 / 0.69; mean 0.739.
   - PdPS-8fea: mean 0.670; SaPS-8fea: mean 0.644; catGRANULE: mean 0.644.
   All 20 ML-classifier × MLO-dataset cells are significant (Mann–Whitney p from 2e-8 down to 1e-268).

2. The same predictors drop to near-chance on membrane-bound controls:
   - Mitochondrial proteome: SaPS-8fea 0.465 (p≈1.0), PdPS-8fea 0.472 (p≈1.0), SaPS-10fea 0.489, PdPS-10fea 0.562, catGRANULE 0.522 — i.e. essentially no MLO-type signal in a membrane-bound organelle.
   - Amyloid fiber-forming proteins: slightly above chance for the 10-feature classifiers (PdPS-10fea 0.602, p=0.003; SaPS-10fea 0.573, p=0.024), consistent with shared aggregation-prone sequence features, but far below MLO values; the 8-feature classifiers are at chance (0.507/0.461).

3. Formal "consistently better" test: mean MLO AUROC minus mean control AUROC is positive for all 7 predictors (PdPS-10fea +0.218, SaPS-10fea +0.208, PdPS-8fea +0.181, SaPS-8fea +0.181, catGRANULE +0.148, PScore +0.029, PLAAC +0.027); one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank across predictors: p = 0.0078 (the minimum possible with n=7). 25 of 28 predictor × MLO-dataset AUROCs exceed the best control AUROC of the same predictor (the 3 exceptions are PScore/PLAAC cells that discriminate nothing).

4. PScore and PLAAC do NOT screen MLOs: PScore AUROC 0.40–0.52 on MLO datasets (e.g. 0.404 on DACT1, p≈1.0; 0.522 on OpenCell, p=0.22); PLAAC 0.34–0.50 (anti-correlated on DACT1, 0.336). Their MLO-vs-control differences (+0.03) are negligible. DeepPhase (available for only 5,333 proteins, 0 PhaSepDB coverage) was likewise inconsistent (0.39–0.59).

5. Screening view: at a threshold admitting 10% of the hNoPS background, PdPS-10fea recovers 38–51% of each MLO dataset (mean 44%) vs 10.6% of the mitochondrial proteome and 21% of amyloid formers; SaPS-10fea recovers 32–40% (mean 35%) vs 6.8%/19%. SaPS-8fea: 22% vs 3.6%/9.7%.

6. PdPS > SaPS on every MLO dataset (e.g. DACT1: 0.832 vs 0.775), consistent with the scaffold/client model: most proteome-scale MLO participants are recruited partner (client) proteins, not self-assembling scaffolds.

7. Robustness: repeating on the "Original data" sheet (training proteins included) inflates AUROCs by 0.001–0.054 without changing any ranking — confirming leakage control matters and the reported numbers are conservative. Using "all non-member proteins" instead of hNoPS as negatives leaves the MLO-minus-control gap intact (e.g. PdPS-10fea 0.766 vs 0.542).

CONCLUSION
PS predictors do perform consistently better on MLO participant datasets than on membrane-bound organelle controls, but the effect is carried by the machine-learning classifiers — especially the 10-feature PdPS and SaPS models (mean MLO AUROC 0.74–0.80 vs 0.53–0.58 on controls, a +0.21 AUROC gap) — and, to a lesser degree, catGRANULE (+0.15). PScore and PLAAC provide essentially no MLO screening power. The mitochondrial control demonstrates that the enrichment is specific to condensate biology rather than generic proteomic detectability, and the weak amyloid signal indicates the 10-feature models partially capture solid-aggregation propensity in addition to liquid–liquid phase separation.

LIMITATIONS
The hNoPS background is defined by absence from the SaPS/PdPS positive sets rather than by experimental non-PS validation; only two control datasets (mitochondria, amyloid) were available; the four MLO datasets are biologically overlapping, so per-dataset AUROCs are not fully independent (mitigated by the predictor-level paired test); and PdPS/SaPS models were trained on interaction/colocalization-type data related in kind to some evaluation sets, although the training-removed sheet eliminates direct protein-level leakage.
grader_notes: The agent's work is thorough and rigorous across most criteria, with only a minor omission in explicitly checking and documenting overlap removal between positive dataset members and the fixed hNoPS background, leading to a B for label construction rather than A.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-11-1: Ligand–receptor communication between KIR+CD8+ T cells and pathogenic CD4+ T cells in celiac disease (GSE193442)

ANALYSIS SUMMARY
All 10 samples (6 active CeD, 4 HC; 72,177 cells, 33,562 genes) were QC-filtered to 69,623 cells, normalized (CP10k + log1p), embedded by TruncatedSVD-PCA and clustered with a 30-NN Jaccard-Louvain pipeline (59 clusters). Marker annotation identified:
- KIR+CD8+ T cells = cluster 12 (n=1,313): CD8A/B+, GNLY/GZMB/GZMH/PRF1-high, TBX21+, ZNF683(Hobit)+, KLRD1+; 56.5% of CeD cells in this cluster express KIR (KIR3DL1/KIR2DL3) vs 34.2% in HC. Sender pool for communication analysis: 436 KIR+CD8 cells from CeD.
- Pathogenic CD4 proxy = cytotoxic CD4+CD8- cells expressing GNLY/PRF1/GZMB/GZMH or NKG7+KLRG1+ (gliadin-specific CD4 T cells in CeD acquire this cytotoxic phenotype; TCR data unavailable). Receiver pool: 931 CeD cells.
A CellPhoneDB/CellChat-style analysis (69 curated LR pairs, complex-min rule, score = mean(ligand)xmean(receptor), 1,000 label permutations, BH-FDR) was run sender=KIR+CD8 -> receiver=pathogenic CD4.

TOP SIGNALING PATHWAYS BEYOND MHC-I (ranked by pathway score / permutation significance):

1. GALECTIN pathway — LGALS1 -> CD69 (top pair: score 1.32, perm p=0.001, padj=0.003). Galectin-1 is expressed by 78% of KIR+CD8 cells and is strongly CeD-induced (padj=1e-23); CD69 is on 47% of pathogenic CD4 cells. Galectin-1 triggers apoptosis and Th1 suppression of activated T cells — the leading candidate for the direct non-MHC-I suppressive arm.

2. CYTOTOXIC-EFFECTOR delivery — GNLY -> PGRMC1 and GZMB -> PGRMC1 (scores 0.32/0.20, padj=0.003). Granulysin (89% of senders) and granzyme B (93% of senders; CeD-upregulated, padj=2e-04) mediate the cytotoxic killing of the targeted CD4 cells seen in vitro.

3. CCL CHEMOKINE recruitment — CCL5 -> CCR4/CCR5, CCL4 -> CCR5, CCL3 -> CCR5 (pathway total 0.449; CCL5 in 100% and CCL4 in 77% of KIR+CD8 cells; all padj=0.003). Recruits/positions pathogenic CD4 cells for contact-dependent suppression.

4. TNF SUPERFAMILY — TNFSF14 (LIGHT) -> TNFRSF14 (HVEM) (score 0.089, padj=0.003). LIGHT is CeD-induced in KIR+CD8 cells (padj=0.015) and HVEM is on 45% of pathogenic CD4 cells; LIGHT-HVEM delivers apoptosis/anti-proliferative signals to activated T cells.

5. DEATH RECEPTOR — FASLG -> FAS (score 0.016, padj=0.003). FASLG is upregulated in CeD KIR+CD8 cells and is a specific feature of the KIR+ population vs other CD8 cells (padj=1e-06); FAS on 12% of pathogenic CD4 cells enables activation-induced cell death.

6. TGF-beta — TGFB1 -> TGFBR1/TGFBR2 (TGFB1 in 55% of senders, KIR+CD8-specific vs other CD8, padj=1e-19; TGFBR2 on 28% of receivers). Soluble immunosuppression of the pathogenic CD4 compartment.

7. ADHESION/CO-RECEPTOR stabilization — CD58 -> CD2 (padj=0.003) stabilizes the effector:target conjugate for granule delivery. CD48 -> CD2 and ICAM3 -> LFA-1 score highly but are NOT population-specific (permutation n.s.) and are best viewed as generic T-cell adhesion.

Benchmark: the established MHC-I -> KIR axis (HLA-A/B/C -> KIR2DL3/3DL1, HLA-E -> KLRC1/KLRD1) aggregated score 0.236 — below the Galectin, SLAM and CCL pathway totals — confirming that pathways beyond MHC-I dominate the predicted suppressive/cytotoxic network.

INTERPRETATION: The data support a multi-layered mechanism in which CeD-expanded KIR+CD8+ T cells (i) home to and conjugate with activated pathogenic CD4 T cells via CCL chemokines and CD58/CD2 adhesion, (ii) suppress them through galectin-1-CD69, LIGHT-HVEM and TGF-beta signaling, and (iii) eliminate them through granulysin/granzyme-B and FASLG-FAS cytotoxicity — complementing the established MHC-I/KIR recognition.

LIMITATIONS: Transcript-level LR inference does not prove protein-level or functional interaction; gliadin specificity is inferred from the cytotoxic CD4 phenotype (no TCR/tetramer data); dropout deflates low-expression checkpoint receptors (PDCD1/CTLA4/TIGIT scored low); single-cell permutation significance is optimistic relative to the 6-vs-4 sample-level statistics; the curated 69-pair LR list is not exhaustive.
grader_notes: The agent performed a thorough analysis with strong QC, clustering, and pathway-level interpretation, but missed UMAP/t-SNE visualization, lacked a dedicated activated CD4 marker set, used fixed thresholds for cell identification, and only computed one-directional LR scoring, leading to minor deductions.

Yes. The G2M checkpoint (MSigDB HALLMARK_G2M_CHECKPOINT) is significantly enriched at p < 0.05 among the DEGs shared between the overexpression (A549) and knockdown (H1299) in-vitro experiments.

Analysis: The two DEG lists in TS7.xlsx (3,260 overexpression DEGs; 5,314 knockdown DEG records, 5,290 unique genes) share 1,543 genes, as marked by the "v" overlap flags in both directions (the two flagged sets are identical; a raw name intersection gives 1,545, differing only by two unflagged genes, AC126755.1 and AC138969.2). Testing over-representation of the 200-gene G2M checkpoint set among these 1,543 shared DEGs against the background of all 7,005 DEGs detected in either experiment (121 G2M genes present in background) gives a 2x2 table of [[37, 1506], [84, 5378]]: 37 of 1,543 shared DEGs (2.40%) are G2M checkpoint genes versus 84 of 5,462 non-shared DEGs (1.54%). A one-sided Fisher's exact test (equivalent to a hypergeometric test) yields odds ratio = 1.57, p = 0.0171 < 0.05. The G2M checkpoint ranks 3rd among all 50 Hallmark sets by nominal p-value (behind HALLMARK_MITOTIC_SPINDLE, p = 2.9e-08, and HALLMARK_UV_RESPONSE_DN, p = 1.9e-04), though it does not survive Benjamini-Hochberg correction across all 50 sets (FDR = 0.286).

Yes. Feminizing GAHT-associated proteins overlap significantly with sex-associated proteins identified in the general population, and the overlap is both enriched and directionally feminizing.

Using the 2,711 proteins measured on both Olink platforms (Supplementary Table 5), 259 proteins changed significantly after 6 months of feminizing GAHT (adj. p < 0.05; 213 in the CPA arm, 81 in the SPIRO arm, 35 shared). Of these, 249 (96.1%) are also sex-associated in the general population (Sun et al. Nature 2023; nominal sex p < 0.05), compared with 88.2% of non-GAHT-responsive proteins — a statistically significant enrichment (Fisher's exact test: odds ratio 3.33, one-sided p = 1.4e-05; CPA alone OR 3.38, p = 6.9e-05; SPIRO alone OR 5.03, p = 4.3e-03). The enrichment matters because plasma protein levels are pervasively sex-differential (89% of measured proteins show a nominal sex difference), so the GAHT set is ~3-5x enriched over an already high background.

The overlap is also directionally consistent with feminization: among GAHT-responsive proteins with a reported sex effect size, the GAHT-induced shift goes toward the female-typical level significantly more often than chance (162/241 arm-level estimates = 67.2%, binomial p = 4.8e-08; CPA hits 63.6%, SPIRO hits 76.5%). Effect sizes correlate positively with population sex betas (Spearman rho 0.18-0.36 across all proteins; 0.43-0.46 among GAHT-significant proteins; all p <= 1e-11). The strongest overlapping proteins are androgen-dependent, male-reproductive-tract proteins whose high male-typical levels collapse toward female levels on GAHT (SPINT3, INSL3, EDDM3B, ACRV1, TEX101, PROK1, MSMB), alongside proteins that rise toward female-typical levels (LEP, PRL).

The overlap is partial, however: only ~10% (249/2,412) of sex-associated proteins respond to 6 months of GAHT, and about one-third of responsive sex-differential proteins do not shift toward female levels. Thus feminizing GAHT remodels a specific, enriched, predominantly female-directed subset of the sex-differential plasma proteome, but does not fully recapitulate population sex differences.
grader_notes: The agent conducted a robust analysis overall but did not follow the rubric's specified top-100 sex-associated protein overlap and hypergeometric testing approach, resulting in major deviations for criteria 2 and 3 and partial deviation for criterion 4.

Are GAHT-induced protein changes consistent with those observed during menopause or menopausal hormone therapy?

ANSWER: GAHT-induced protein changes are consistent with menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) but OPPOSITE to menopause. Feminizing GAHT directionally reproduces the plasma-protein signature of estrogen-replacement therapy in postmenopausal women and reverses the signature of estrogen withdrawal at menopause.

KEY EVIDENCE (258 GAHT-regulated proteins, FDR<0.05, from Supplementary Table 1; comparator associations from Supplementary Table 7):

1. The GAHT signature is dominated by down-regulation: 245 of 258 proteins (95.0%) decrease after 6 months of GAHT; only 13 increase (leptin, LEP, is the largest increase, +1.27 NPX, significant under both CPA and SPIRO). CPA- and SPIRO-regulated proteins are mutually direction-concordant (34/34 shared proteins same sign).

2. Consistency WITH MHT: 72.1% (MHT, age <57) and 80.2% (MHT, age >=57) of GAHT proteins change in the same direction under MHT (exact binomial p = 8.4e-13 and 1.8e-23 vs the 50% null). Among proteins significant for BOTH GAHT and MHT, concordance rises to 80.1% (113/141, p = 2.6e-13) and 92.3% (108/117, p = 1.1e-22); the shared signature is joint down-regulation (MHT lowers 104-111 of these proteins, as does GAHT).

3. INconsistency with menopause: only 14.7% overall sign concordance (38/258, p = 2.5e-32, significantly BELOW chance); among the 222 GAHT proteins also significant for menopause (<57 y), concordance collapses to 10.4% (23/222, p = 3.7e-36) because menopause UP-regulates 197/222 of the proteins that GAHT down-regulates. Menopause in the >=57 stratum shows no relationship (49.6% concordance, p = 0.95).

4. Hormone-axis attribution: GAHT changes track the female ln-estradiol association profile (72.1% overall; 84.9% among doubly-significant proteins, with estradiol effects predominantly negative like GAHT) and are ANTI-concordant with ln-testosterone in both females (28.1% concordant among doubly-significant, p = 3.1e-06) and males (37.8%, p = 1.3e-03). They do not track male estradiol profiles (0/258 significant; 21.7% concordance). This is exactly the pattern expected from an intervention that raises estradiol and suppresses androgens.

5. Robustness: the pattern holds in both antiandrogen regimens (CPA arm: 69-79% concordance with MHT, 15% with menopause; SPIRO arm: 82-85% with MHT, 20% with menopause), so it is not specific to cyproterone acetate.

6. Representative proteins in the shared GAHT-MHT signature: up-regulated LEP (leptin) and SERPINA12 (vaspin); down-regulated PROK1, MMP3, SSC4D, BPIFA2, CA6, MSMB, OBP2B, TOP1, SCRG1, CKB, IGFBP2, FGF23 and REN - adipokines, extracellular-matrix/protease and metabolic proteins responsive to sex steroids.

INTERPRETATION: Menopause (estradiol deficiency) and feminizing GAHT (estradiol repletion plus androgen suppression) push the same protein set in opposite directions, while MHT (pharmacologic estrogen repletion) pushes it in the same direction as GAHT. At the plasma-proteome level, 6 months of feminizing GAHT therefore mirrors MHT and counteracts the menopausal protein signature, consistent with an estradiol-driven feminizing program.

LIMITATIONS: concordance is at the sign level (Spearman correlations of effect magnitudes are weak, |rho| <= 0.17); GAHT models had only n=20 per arm versus much larger cisgender comparator cohorts; menopause is a composite of aging and hormonal change (the >=57 stratum showed no signal); only FDR-adjusted p-values were available (no standard errors for precision weighting); and Olink NPX values are relative abundances, so absolute concentration changes cannot be inferred.
grader_notes: The agent performed a robust analysis with appropriate data handling, matching, and quantification, and gave an excellent biological interpretation, but failed to identify and characterize notable discordant proteins, instead focusing on concordant examples, which is a significant omission per the rubric.

synaptic decline. This supports glial (especially microglial) activation as a candidate
molecular driver of ALS pathology.

LIMITATIONS
Bulk tissue cannot fully separate per-cell regulation from cell-composition change (neuron
loss inflates glial fractions); postmortem end-stage tissue precludes causal ordering; the

Yes. Weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA) of the pooled postmortem ALS spinal-cord RNA-seq cohort (377 samples after QC: 297 ALS, 80 non-neurological controls across cervical, lumbar and thoracic levels; 8,000 top-MAD genes from DESeq2 VST-normalized, covariate-adjusted expression; signed bicor network, soft-threshold power 6, scale-free R^2 = 0.94) resolved 9 discrete co-expression modules (124-3,890 genes, zero unassigned), three of which are significantly dysregulated in ALS (module-eigengene vs disease, BH-adjusted p < 0.05, |r| > 0.2):

1. green module (425 genes) — UP in ALS (r = +0.38, padj = 8.3e-14). A microglial/innate-immune program: top GO terms inflammatory response, cytokine production, regulation of immune response (padj ~1e-22 to 1e-18); hub genes FPR1, C1QA/C1QB/C1QC, CD163, C5AR1, LILRB3, GPNMB, ALOX5AP, TYROBP; enriched 24/44 for Mathys microglial markers (padj = 6.6e-18). Replicates within cervical (partial r = +0.46, p = 1.8e-10) and lumbar (r = +0.36, p = 6.0e-6) cord after controlling RIN, age and sex. This is the transcriptomic signature of ALS glial activation/neuroinflammation.

2. turquoise module (3,890 genes) — DOWN in ALS (r = -0.21, padj = 7.9e-05). A pan-neuronal synaptic program: GO terms trans-synaptic signaling, chemical synaptic transmission, synaptic vesicle cycle (padj ~1e-17 to 1e-6); hub genes NEFM/NEFL/NEFH, INA, GRIN1, CPLX2, SLC12A5, ATP1A3; enriched for excitatory (44/50) and inhibitory (49/56) neuronal markers. Strongest in cervical cord (partial r = -0.31, p = 2.3e-5) and also lower in C9orf72 carriers (r = -0.20, padj = 0.001). Consistent with motor-neuron loss and synaptic degeneration.

3. brown module (830 genes) — DOWN in ALS (r = -0.39, padj = 7.8e-14), the single strongest eigengene-disease association; replicates in cervical (-0.44) and lumbar (-0.37). No enriched GO term; contains oligodendrocyte-lineage genes (e.g., BCAS1) and many uncharacterized transcripts, suggesting a heterogeneous homeostatic/myelin-related program eroded in ALS.

Weaker disease associations were seen for yellow (endothelial/apoptotic, r = -0.15, padj = 0.009) and black (pericyte/ECM/vasculature, r = +0.12, padj = 0.036), pointing to neurovascular involvement. No module was associated with sex or age after correction, and residual RIN signal was confined to a disease-neutral module, confirming that covariate adjustment isolated the disease biology.

Interpretation: WGCNA identifies coordinated gene programs in ALS spinal cord dominated by a reciprocal axis of microglial immune/complement activation (up) and neuronal synaptic/neurofilament expression (down), plus a downregulated myelin/homeostasis program — matching the glial-activation and neuronal-loss duality reported for ALS spinal cord. Limitations: bulk data cannot fully separate cell-composition change from within-cell regulation; associations are correlational and postmortem; the thoracic level is underpowered (n = 52), so formal replication is limited to cervical and lumbar cord.
grader_notes: The analysis is technically strong and well-documented, but it fails the core requirement of ALS-only WGCNA by including control samples, and it lacks PCA-based QC plots, resulting in penalties on the first two criteria.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-15-7: Genes most strongly correlated with ALS disease duration

METHOD (summary)
Per spinal-cord region (cervical n=120, lumbar n=99, thoracic n=40 ALS samples with recorded disease duration), each expressed gene (TPM >= 1 in >= 25% of samples; log2(TPM+1); ~13,000 genes per region) was correlated with disease duration (years, onset to death) by Spearman rank correlation with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR, then combined across regions with a sample-size-weighted Stouffer meta-analysis. Note the sign convention: shorter duration = faster progression, so a NEGATIVE correlation marks genes associated with RAPID progression.

TOP ANSWER
CHIT1 (chitinase-1 / chitotriosidase) is the single strongest and most consistent gene: Spearman rho = -0.513 (p = 2.1e-9, FDR = 2.7e-5) cervical, rho = -0.451 (p = 2.8e-6, FDR = 0.036) lumbar, rho = -0.487 (nominal p = 1.6e-3) thoracic; cross-region meta-analysis p = 1.9e-16, FDR = 2.4e-12. Higher CHIT1 expression in spinal cord at death is associated with shorter disease duration, i.e., faster ALS progression. The association survives adjustment for age, sex, RIN and genotype PCs (partial rho = -0.568, p = 1.4e-11), removal of ultra-rapid (duration = 0) cases, and exclusion of C9orf72 mutation carriers.

THE NEXT STRONGEST GENES (all negative correlation = fast progression; all replicated, same direction, across cervical/lumbar/thoracic; meta-FDR < 3e-6):
  RAB42 (rho -0.37 / -0.39 / -0.51; meta p = 4.8e-11)
  DPEP2 (-0.38 / -0.37 / -0.42; p = 2.6e-10)
  OAS1 (-0.46 / -0.29 / -0.35; p = 3.0e-10)
  UNC93B1 (-0.41 / -0.37 / -0.28; p = 6.1e-10)
  PLA2G7 (-0.36 / -0.35 / -0.47; p = 7.2e-10)
  PYCARD (-0.38 / -0.38 / -0.33; p = 1.1e-9)
  MX2 (-0.43 / -0.30 / -0.35; p = 1.3e-9)
  GPNMB (-0.37 / -0.33 / -0.46; p = 1.6e-9)
  CAPG (-0.39 / -0.35 / -0.32; p = 2.3e-9)
  (further FDR<0.05: APOC2, CEBPA, CD37, LSP1, FBP1, DOK3, PLAU, NCF2, SLC29A1, LILRA2, CHI3L1 — 400 genes total at meta-FDR < 0.05; 390 of them negatively correlated with duration)

INTERPRETATION
The duration-correlated transcriptome is an innate-immune / microglial-macrophage neuroinflammation signature: chitinase-family proteins (CHIT1, CHI3L1), type-I-interferon-stimulated genes (OAS1, MX2, EPSTI1), inflammasome/TLR components (PYCARD/ASC, UNC93B1, NCF2), and myeloid markers (GPNMB, CAPG, LSP1, CD37, LILRA2). Thus the degree of glial/innate-immune activation in spinal cord tracks how fast the disease progressed. This is consistent with independent protein-level evidence that CSF CHIT1 and CHI3L1 (YKL-40) predict ALS progression rate (Thompson et al., Ann Clin Transl Neurol 2018, PMID 29932231; Steinacker et al., Acta Neuropathol Commun 2018, doi:10.1186/s40478-018-0545-4; Oeckl et al., Acta Neuropathol 2019). Genes positively correlated with duration (slower progression) are few and weaker (best: IL17D, IGSF1, SELL, meta-FDR < 0.02).

CAVEATS
Postmortem end-stage tissue cannot establish that these genes prospectively predict progression during life (reverse causation: fast progressors have more advanced microgliosis at death); bulk RNA-seq correlations partly reflect cell-composition shifts; the thoracic cohort (n=40) is individually underpowered (nothing passes region-specific FDR, though directionally concordant); proteomics files were not present in this workspace, so orthogonal protein validation relied on published literature rather than re-analysis.
grader_notes: The agent's continuous disease-duration correlation analysis is well-executed and biologically interpretable, with strong CHIT1 identification and validation. However, it deviates substantially from the required voom+limma framework by using TPM+Spearman correlation without quantile/TMM normalization or covariate-adjusted linear modeling, which lowers criteria 2 and 3.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-16-1: Molecular subtypes of NAFLD by unsupervised clustering

Yes. Unsupervised clustering of the 206 NAFLD hepatic transcriptomes in GSE135251
(10 healthy controls excluded) does stratify patients by disease severity — but only
after the dominant technical source of variation is handled, because the leading
principal component (PC1, 34.9% of variance) is a library-size/technical axis
(Spearman r with library size = -0.48, p = 4e-13) with no association to fibrosis
(p = 0.39), NAS (p = 0.35), or early/moderate stage (p = 0.68). Clustering that
includes PC1 finds clusters with NO severity association. The disease-severity signal
lives in PC2–PC6 (e.g. PC5 vs fibrosis r = +0.47, p = 8.6e-13; PC2 vs NAS r = +0.43,
p = 1.7e-10).

METHOD. Per-sample HTSeq counts (216 files; 5 HTSeq summary rows per file dropped) were
assembled into a 64,253-gene matrix, normalized to CPM, filtered to genes with CPM >= 1
in >= 20 samples (14,875 genes), log2(CPM+1) transformed, reduced to the top 5,000
most variable genes (MAD), z-scored, and subjected to PCA. Ward hierarchical clustering
was performed on Euclidean distances in PC2–PC10 space. Silhouette was best at k = 3
(0.173; clusters of 88, 73, 45 cases).

KEY RESULT (k = 3; clusters relabeled by ascending severity):
- Fibrosis stage: chi-square p = 1.1e-4 (Cramer's V = 0.25); Kruskal-Wallis p = 8.0e-7;
  medians C1 = F1, C2 = F2, C3 = F3. Pairwise: C1 vs C3 p = 8.4e-8, C2 vs C3 p = 1.0e-4.
- NAS score: Kruskal-Wallis p = 4.0e-7; medians C1 = 4, C2 = 5, C3 = 6.
- Early/moderate stage: chi-square p = 6.4e-6; moderate fraction rises 20.5% (C1) ->
  30.1% (C2) -> 62.2% (C3).
- Group in paper: chi-square p = 1.8e-4; C3 is enriched for NASH_F3 (21/54) and NASH_F4
  (7/14) and depleted of NAFL (4/51).
- k = 4 gives the same gradient (fibrosis KW p = 4.9e-8; stage chi-square p = 6.7e-6).

INTERPRETATION. The three transcriptomic clusters form a severity gradient, not discrete
islands (silhouettes are modest, 0.16–0.17, as expected for a continuous disease
spectrum): C1 = mild (predominantly F0–F2, NAFL, early), C2 = intermediate, C3 =
advanced fibrotic NASH (median F3, NAS 6, 62% "moderate"). Cluster C3 is driven by the
canonical hepatic stellate-cell activation / extracellular-matrix / inflammatory program
(LUM, DCN, THBS2, PALLD, GPC4, CCL2, CCL20, SERPINE2, LXN among the top
differentially expressed genes), i.e. a fibrogenic, inflammation-high molecular subtype.

CLINICAL-TRIAL IMPLICATION. A C3-like transcriptional signature could enrich trials for
advanced-fibrosis/high-NAS patients, but enrichment is imperfect (6 of 45 C3 patients are
F0–F1, and 25 advanced-fibrosis patients fall outside C3), so it would supplement, not
replace, histology. Because severity-carrying PCs were identified in the same cohort,
these associations require validation in an independent NAFLD cohort before use.

Deliverables: analysis/fig1_clusters.png (scree, PCA, fibrosis/NAS by cluster, stage
composition); analysis/metadata.csv, analysis/meta_final.csv (per-sample cluster labels);
analysis/DE_C3_vs_rest.csv (cluster-driver genes). See trace.md for full methods, code,
and references.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-17-1: Circulating immune cell populations with significantly altered frequencies in SLE

Analysis of the 1,263,676-cell PBMC scRNA-seq cohort (162 SLE donors, 99 healthy donors; donor-level quasi-binomial GLM on cell counts with Mann–Whitney and arcsin-sqrt t-test confirmation; Benjamini–Hochberg FDR across 11 populations) identifies FIVE immune cell populations with significantly and robustly altered circulating frequencies in SLE:

INCREASED in SLE:
1. Classical monocytes (cM): 28.5% vs 18.1% of PBMCs (log2FC +0.66, q = 2.3e-15)
2. Non-classical monocytes (ncM): 4.3% vs 3.0% (log2FC +0.52, q = 6.3e-05)
3. Proliferating lymphocytes (Prolif): 0.87% vs 0.38% (log2FC +1.19, q = 1.6e-08)

DECREASED in SLE:
4. CD4+ alpha-beta T cells (T4): 24.8% vs 37.5% (log2FC -0.60, q = 7.5e-20)
5. Plasmacytoid dendritic cells (pDC): 0.30% vs 0.57% (log2FC -0.93, q = 6.4e-17)

All five remain significant (FDR < 0.05) after sex adjustment, restriction to the ethnicity-balanced European-American subset (74 SLE / 75 HC), and exclusion of all flare donors, so they are not driven by demographic imbalance or acute flare.

NOT significantly altered: B cells (q = 0.61) and plasmablasts (q = 0.38). CD8 T cells, NK cells, conventional dendritic cells, and progenitor cells give discordant results across tests (significant in at most 2 of 3 methods; the CD8 signal vanishes in European Americans, indicating an ethnicity artifact) and are not robust biomarker candidates at this annotation level.

Interpretation for SLE diagnosis: the strongest cellular signature of SLE in blood is a myeloid expansion (classical + non-classical monocytes) together with contraction of CD4+ T cells and circulating pDCs and an excess of proliferating lymphocytes. These shifts are consistent with the type-I interferon-driven immune activation of SLE (interferon-activated monocyte expansion, lymphopenia, and pDC migration out of blood into inflamed tissues). A composite of monocyte-high / CD4-low / pDC-low frequencies would be the strongest candidate circulating cellular biomarker panel from this cohort. Caveats: frequencies are compositional (monocyte expansion dilutes other fractions), most patients were on immunosuppressive treatment, and the cohort is predominantly female — absolute-count and longitudinal validation would be needed before clinical use.
grader_notes: The agent performed a rigorous donor-level statistical analysis with multiple testing correction and proper biological interpretation, but missed several expected significant cell types and did not address low-count filtering per cell type.

Do SLE-associated immune cell changes differ between patients of Asian versus European ancestry?

Answer: Largely shared, but with one clear ancestry difference — CD4 T-cell depletion is significantly stronger in Asian SLE patients — plus directional evidence of a stronger interferon response in Asians.

Analysis of 1.24M PBMCs (149 European-American and 107 Asian donors; 75 EUR / 83 ASN SLE cases vs 74 EUR / 24 ASN healthy controls), aggregated per donor and per cell type and modeled with covariate-adjusted (age, sex, processing cohort) ancestry x disease interaction tests:

1) SHARED changes (similar in both ancestries): classical and non-classical monocyte expansion (cM ~0.19->0.29 EUR, 0.16->0.28 ASN), proliferating-cell expansion, regulatory CD4 T-cell expansion, memory B-cell depletion, cytotoxic T-cell expansion, and a significant type-I interferon-stimulated-gene (ISG) induction in every well-powered cell type (largest in monocytes, +1.5 to +1.9 log2). This core myeloid-interferon SLE axis supports ancestry-agnostic interferon-targeted therapy (e.g., anifrolumab).

2) ANCESTRY-DIFFERENTIAL change: CD4 T-cell depletion is significantly more pronounced in Asian patients (interaction p=0.0058). In proportions, Asian cases lose roughly half of their naive CD4 compartment vs Asian controls (0.36->0.16), versus a milder drop in Europeans (0.35->0.23); the fine-subtype decomposition shows the effect is driven by naive CD4 T cells (interaction p=0.012) and MAIT cells (interaction p=0.025). Asian controls also have a higher baseline CD4 fraction (0.42 vs 0.36), so population-specific reference ranges may matter clinically.

3) DIRECTIONAL but not significant: the ISG elevation in SLE is consistently larger in Asians across all 8 well-powered cell types (interaction betas +0.29 to +0.65 log2; smallest adjusted interaction p=0.053 in conventional dendritic cells), suggesting a modestly stronger interferon response in Asian SLE, consistent with the higher SLE prevalence/severity reported in Asian populations — but it does not reach significance in any single cell type. Other nominal hints: pDC depletion is dramatic in Europeans (p=2e-10) but undetectable in Asians (who already have low baseline pDC fractions), and B-cell fraction decreases only in Europeans while atypical B cells expand significantly only in Asians; none of these interactions survive multiple-testing correction.

Limitations: only 24 Asian healthy controls limit power (interaction q-values > 0.05 after FDR, so findings are hypothesis-generating); ethnicity is self-reported; processing cohort is partially confounded with ancestry; compositional fractions are relative; rare cell types are underpowered; and without genotypes we cannot distinguish genetic from environmental drivers of the ancestry differences.

Bottom line for population-specific treatment strategies: the dominant SLE immune program (monocyte expansion + interferon activation) is shared across Asian and European patients, but Asian patients show significantly deeper naive CD4/MAIT T-cell depletion and a trend toward stronger interferon induction, which may warrant ancestry-aware immune-monitoring thresholds and further powered studies of interferon-pathway targeting in Asian SLE.
grader_notes: The agent conducts a thorough ancestry-stratified analysis with appropriate formal testing and source grounding; minor deductions for not filtering low-count donors in composition estimates and for an Asian CD4 fold change deviating from the rubric's expected range.

The four clinical receptor subtypes have sharply distinct and largely
non-overlapping genomic drivers. HR+ disease is defined by PI3K-pathway and
ER-axis alterations plus the 11q13 (CCND1/FGF) amplicon; HER2+ disease is
amplification-driven (ERBB2/17q12) with a high TP53 burden; TNBC is a
TP53/RB1-loss, PI3K-pathway-loss, MYC-amplified disease with the highest
tumor mutational burden.

1. TUMOR MUTATIONAL BURDEN
Median TMB (nonsynonymous mut/Mb): HR+HER2- 0.100, HR+HER2+ 0.100,
HR-HER2+ 0.133, TNBC 0.167 (Kruskal-Wallis p = 1.8e-9; TNBC vs HR+HER2-
Mann-Whitney p = 1.8e-9). The gradient holds within primary-only
(p = 5.5e-4) and metastatic-only (p = 2.9e-4) strata, so it is not a
treatment-selection artifact. On this targeted panel virtually no sample
(1/1,814) reaches TMB >= 10 mut/Mb.

2. NONSYNONYMOUS MUTATIONS (frequency % by subtype; BH-FDR < 0.05)
- TP53: 23.3 / 47.0 / 78.6 / 81.2 - HER2+ and especially TNBC enriched.
- PIK3CA: 42.5 / 31.8 / 32.9 / 18.8 - HR+HER2- enriched (H1047R, E545K,
  E542K hotspots; alpelisib-actionable).
- AKT1: 6.4 / 0 / 1.4 / 4.0 - HR+HER2- enriched (84 of 93 variants are
  E17K; capivasertib-actionable).
- GATA3: 18.0 / 12.1 / 2.9 / 3.6 and MAP3K1: 9.8 / 2.3 / 2.9 / 4.8 -
  luminal/HR+ specific.
- CDH1: 18.5 / 12.1 / 7.1 / 8.0 - HR+ (lobular histology).
- ESR1: 10.3 / 6.1 / 0 / 0.4 - restricted to HR+ disease; dominated by
  ligand-binding-domain hotspots D538G, Y537S/N/C, E380Q, L536H/P that
  drive endocrine resistance. Within HR+HER2-, ESR1 mutations are enriched
  ~9-fold in metastases vs primaries (19.2% vs 2.6%; Fisher OR 8.95,
  p = 1.9e-25), reflecting hormonal-therapy selection; PIK3CA and TP53
  show no such shift, confirming the effect is endocrine-specific.
- RB1: 1.8 / 1.5 / 0 / 11.2 - TNBC enriched.
- PIK3R1: 0.8 / 1.5 / 4.3 / 8.0 and NF1: 3.5 / 5.3 / 11.4 / 8.0 -
  enriched in HR-HER2+ and TNBC.
- RECQL4: 0.9 / 1.5 / 7.1 / 0.4 - HR-HER2+ enriched.
- Not subtype-specific: PTEN (3-9%) and ERBB2 (4-7%) mutations.

3. COPY-NUMBER ALTERATIONS
- HER2+ subtypes are amplification-driven: ERBB2 amplified in 79.5%
  (HR+HER2+) and 90.0% (HR-HER2+) vs 0.4% (HR+HER2-) and 0% (TNBC), with
  17q12 CDK12 co-amplification in ~55-60% and RARA (17q21) in up to 25%.
  Overall CNA burden is significantly higher in both HER2+ groups
  (Kruskal-Wallis p = 2.5e-21).
- HR+ disease carries the 11q13 amplicon: CCND1 21.6%/22.7% and
  FGF3/FGF4/FGF19 18-21% in HR+ vs 4-7% in HER2+/TNBC; FGFR1 amplified in
  14.0% of HR+HER2-.
- TNBC: MYC amplification 15.6% (highest), RB1 deep deletion 5.6% and
  PTEN deep deletion 4.4% (vs <=0.3% and <=1.8% in HR+), complementing its
  TP53/RB1-loss mutation profile.
- CDKN2A/B deep deletions are rare (2-6%) and not subtype-specific.

4. ACTIONABLE SUBCOHORTS REVEALED BY MUTATIONAL PROFILING
- Within clinically HER2-negative (HR+HER2-) tumors, ~3.9% carry ERBB2
  kinase-domain hotspot mutations (L755S, V777L, S310F, exon-20
  insertions), almost mutually exclusive with ERBB2 amplification (1/53
  overlap) - a neratinib-sensitive subcohort invisible to receptor IHC.
- PIK3CA mutations in 19-43% across all subtypes and AKT1 E17K in 6.4% of
  HR+HER2- define PI3K/AKT-inhibitor-eligible subcohorts.
- ESR1 LBD mutations in ~19% of post-endocrine-therapy HR+ metastases
  predict benefit from oral SERDs (e.g. elacestrant).
- Small BRCA1/2-mutant fractions exist in every subtype (BRCA2 1.5-4.3%).

5. LIMITATIONS
Targeted panel (~450-474 genes): no genome-wide signatures, HRD scores, or
exome-scale TMB; CNA file reports only high-level amplifications and deep
deletions (no shallow gains/losses or LOH); 55% of samples are metastases
from an endocrine-therapy-enriched cohort, so alteration frequencies
reflect post-treatment disease rather than incidence at diagnosis; power is
limited for HR-HER2+ (n=70); 104 samples (5.4%) were excluded for
unknown/equivocal receptor status; some patients contribute >1 sample.

CONCLUSION
Receptor subtypes partition breast cancer into genomically distinct
diseases: HR+HER2- = PIK3CA/AKT1 + ER-axis (GATA3, MAP3K1, CDH1) mutations
with 11q13 amplification and therapy-selected ESR1 LBD mutations;
HR+HER2+ and HR-HER2+ = ERBB2/17q12-amplified, TP53-rich (47-79%),
amplification-burdened tumors; TNBC = TP53 (81%) and RB1 loss, PI3K-pathway
loss (PIK3R1/PTEN), MYC amplification, and the highest TMB. Mutational
profiling additionally unmasks actionable subcohorts within each clinical
group - most notably ERBB2 kinase mutations in HER2-negative disease,
PI3K/AKT-pathway targets in HR+ tumors, and endocrine-resistance ESR1
mutations in treated HR+ metastases.

Breakdown: 203/762 (26.6%) had a MAPK pathway mutation, 78/762 (10.2%) had a relevant copy-number alteration, 26 samples had both. Answer: approximately one-third (33.5%, 255/762) of post-hormonal therapy HR+/HER2- tumors harbor a MAPK pathway alteration.

ESR1 mutations and MAPK pathway alterations are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE in post-hormonal-therapy HR+/HER2- breast tumors.

Cohort: 680 post-hormonal-therapy HR+/HER2- patients (metastases + post-treatment/post-neoadjuvant primaries; one sample per patient; 648 with sequencing records) from the MSK-IMPACT endocrine-resistant breast cancer cohort. Oncogenic ESR1 ligand-binding-domain hotspot mutations (Y537S/N/C/D, D538G, E380Q, L536H/P/Q/R, S463P, etc.) were found in 90/648 tumors (13.9%) — versus 0/619 treatment-naive HR+/HER2- primaries, confirming therapy-driven selection.

Key findings:
- Against a curated RTK-RAS-MAPK definition (NF1 loss-of-function mutation or deep deletion; activating KRAS/NRAS/HRAS/BRAF/MAP2K1 mutation; KRAS/NRAS/BRAF/RAF1 amplification), only 1 of 49 MAPK-altered tumors also carries an ESR1 mutation: odds ratio 0.12, Fisher's exact p = 0.009 (metastasis-only subset: OR 0.14, p = 0.020).
- The exclusivity is driven specifically by NF1 loss: 31 tumors carry NF1 loss-of-function mutations or deep deletions, and ZERO overlap with ESR1 mutations (OR = 0.00, p = 0.015; metastasis-only p = 0.038). NF1 missense mutations of uncertain significance also rarely co-occur (1/41, OR 0.15, p = 0.032).
- A broad 12-gene "any alteration" MAPK definition still shows significant depletion (OR 0.55, p = 0.046), but the signal is diluted because MAP3K1 and MAP2K4 alterations co-occur with ESR1 at rates consistent with independence (OR ~0.8-2.1, p > 0.2) — they do not participate in the exclusivity.

Interpretation: ESR1 ligand-binding-domain mutations and NF1-loss/RAS-RAF-MAPK-pathway activation are two largely non-overlapping, independent genomic routes to endocrine resistance in HR+/HER2- breast cancer. Tumors that hyperactivate MAPK signaling do not acquire ESR1 mutations, and vice versa. This defines an ESR1-wild-type, MAPK-driven resistant subgroup (≈7.6% of post-therapy tumors) that would not benefit from next-generation SERDs targeting mutant ER but may be candidates for MAPK-pathway-directed therapy.

Question: Which genes are most significantly downregulated upon AI-10-49 treatment of ME-1 inv(16) AML cells?

RUNX1 chromatin occupancy increases massively and redistributes upon CBFβ-SMMHC inhibition with AI-10-49 in ME-1 inv(16) AML cells; the drug does not remove RUNX1 from chromatin — it releases it onto thousands of new sites.

Key quantitative findings (MACS2 narrowPeak, IP vs matched input):

1. RUNX1 peak count rises 6.9-fold: 1,328 peaks in DMSO (GSM2715537) vs 9,166 in AI-10-49 (GSM2715538, standard chromosomes). Median peak signal rises from 5.42 to 7.21 fold-enrichment and median qValue from 12.19 to 15.69; median peak width grows 222 -> 295 bp.

2. The change is dominated by GAIN of binding, not loss. Across the 9,266 merged union regions: 7,950 (85.8%) are AI-10-49-only (gained), 1,219 (13.2%) are shared, and only 97 (1.0%) are DMSO-only (lost). 92.7% (1,232/1,329) of DMSO peaks are retained after treatment. At shared sites occupancy gets STRONGER: median signal 5.48 (DMSO) -> 12.53 (AI-10-49), ~2.2-fold, with 93% of shared regions gaining signal.

3. Gained RUNX1 sites target active regulatory elements: 34.8% of gained peaks fall within promoters (TSS +/- 2 kb; ~47% within 10 kb of a TSS), and 90.0% overlap regions already marked by H3K27ac in untreated (DMSO) cells. Thus liberated RUNX1 loads onto the pre-existing active promoter/enhancer landscape rather than pioneering closed chromatin.

4. The post-treatment RUNX1 cistrome maps to 5,566 nearest protein-coding genes (2,800 via promoter-proximal peaks), enriched for leukemia-relevant regulators: MYC (a NEW promoter peak 56 bp from the MYC TSS at chr8:128,747,329-128,747,624, plus stronger binding at the ~128.93 Mb element where signal rises 5.2 -> 16.3), BCL2, CCND2, STAT3, STAT5A, FOS, JUN, CDKN1A, GATA2, MYB, KIT, CSF1R, MPO, and differentiation factors SMAD7, ID2, NCOR2, BCOR.

5. H3K27ac is globally stable (57,784 vs 56,277 peaks, ratio 0.97; 71% of DMSO peaks retained) with selective attenuation at some loci (e.g. MYC promoter qValue 178 -> 77 at essentially unchanged signal), so the therapeutic response is driven by redistribution of RUNX1 onto active chromatin, not wholesale chromatin shutdown.

Interpretation: CBFβ-SMMHC binds and sequesters RUNX1 off chromatin; AI-10-49 disrupts the CBFβ-SMMHC-RUNX1 interaction, so RUNX1 is released and its genomic occupancy expands ~7-fold, with >85% of all occupied regions being newly gained and pre-existing sites gaining signal. The RUNX1 targets that mediate AI-10-49's therapeutic effect are therefore the roughly 8,000 gained RUNX1-binding sites at promoters/enhancers of proliferation and survival genes (MYC, BCL2, CCND2, STAT3/5A) and myeloid differentiation regulators (GATA2, MYB, ID2, MPO), through which restored RUNX1 activity rewires the leukemic transcriptional program toward apoptosis and differentiation.

Caveats: single ChIP replicate per condition precludes formal differential-binding statistics; a small part of the peak-count difference could reflect library/enrichment differences; distal gained peaks are assigned by nearest-TSS heuristic. All numbers were derived directly from the provided narrowPeak files and GENCODE v19 annotation.
grader_notes: The agent robustly performs RUNX1-peak selection, differential occupancy counting, and mechanistic interpretation, but its genomic feature enrichment analysis is incomplete because it lacks the four-class annotation, precedence rule, and formal statistical test against unchanged peaks required for full marks.

Yes — AI-10-49 treatment leads to a global, genome-wide change in chromatin accessibility in inv(16) ME-1 cells, characterized by a moderate net CONTRACTION of the accessible landscape (biased toward loss of open sites) together with widespread bidirectional remodeling, while a large core of accessible sites is preserved.

Quantitative evidence from the four ATAC-seq samples (MACS2 narrowPeak, q<0.05):

1) Fewer accessible sites genome-wide. AI-10-49 replicates yield 48,706 and 53,141 peaks vs 67,066 and 64,929 for DMSO — 23% fewer despite the AI-10-49 libraries being ~1.7x deeper (4.1-4.4M vs 2.5M MACS2 fragments). After normalizing for sequencing depth, the accessible-site count drops to ~45% of DMSO (ratio 0.450). Total accessible base pairs shrink from ~8.5 Mb (DMSO mean) to ~7.4 Mb (AI-10-49 mean) even without depth correction.

2) Widespread peak turnover, slightly biased toward loss. Of 63,001 robust consensus sites (peaks in both replicates of at least one condition), 28,895 (46%, dominating by base pairs) are shared by all four samples; 17,680 are DMSO-only (lost after treatment) and 16,426 are AI-10-49-only (gained). Loss modestly exceeds gain (ratio 1.08; binomial p = 1.2e-11), so the change is a genome-wide remodeling with net closing rather than a wholesale collapse or a purely focal effect.

3) Quantitative signal confirms a mild global decrease. Across all 128,379 consensus regions, depth-normalized (CPM) ATAC signal shifts down: median log2(CPM+1) 1.68 (DMSO) vs 1.46 (AI-10-49); median log2 fold change = -0.278; paired Wilcoxon signed-rank p < 2.2e-16. 23.9% of regions lose >=2-fold accessibility vs 14.0% gaining >=2-fold; at the >=4-fold tail, gains and losses are balanced (5,234 vs 5,144), showing the strongest changes are locus-specific in both directions while the bulk of the genome shifts modestly downward. Remaining AI-10-49 peaks are wider (median ~118 vs ~103 bp) and stronger (median signalValue ~6.8 vs ~5.3), consistent with preferential loss of weak/marginal open sites.

4) Locus-level check: peaks within MYC +/-500 kb (hg19) drop from 54/54 (DMSO rep1/2) to 39/36 (AI-10-49 rep1/2), consistent with AI-10-49 disrupting RUNX1/CBFbeta-SMMHC-driven MYC enhancer accessibility.

In summary: CBFbeta-SMMHC inhibition by AI-10-49 causes a statistically significant global reduction and redistribution of chromatin accessibility — tens of thousands of sites change in both directions with a net bias toward closing (~0.28 log2 median genome-wide shift, ~23% fewer called sites) — rather than leaving the chromatin landscape unchanged or affecting only isolated loci. Limitations: only n=2 replicates per condition and peak-level (not BAM-level) data, so per-site differential statistics are descriptive and global inference is distributional; peaks were called at a lenient q<0.05; depth normalization is linear/approximate.

BASELINE TRANSCRIPTIONAL SIGNATURES OF THE FOUR PRIMARY CELL TYPES (GDPx2 Drug-seq cohort)

Summary answer: The four primary cell types show clearly DISTINCT, essentially non-overlapping baseline
transcriptional signatures. The platform passes this validation step: every DMSO baseline sample can be
assigned to its correct cell type with 100% accuracy. The two most similar cell types are skeletal muscle
myoblasts (SkMMs) and dermal fibroblasts; the three mesenchymal/muscle types (fibroblasts, myoblasts,
aortic smooth muscle cells) cluster together, with melanocytes as the clear outgroup.

METHODS (brief)
- Baseline = all 576 unique DMSO vehicle-control samples (sample_type "Ginkgo Neg Control - DMSO",
  24 h), 144 per cell type. After removing 3 failed wells (<100k UMIs; all AoSMC), n = 573
  (AoSMC 141, Fibroblast 144, Melanocyte 144, SkMyoblast 144).
- Gene filtering (>=5 UMIs in >=10 samples) retained 13,468 of 59,427 genes; normalized as log2(CPM+1).
- PCA on the 2,000 most variable genes; similarity quantified by centroid Pearson correlations
  (all 13,468 genes), average-linkage hierarchical clustering, PERMANOVA (999 permutations),
  silhouette score, and leave-one-out nearest-centroid classification.

RESULTS
1. Distinctness of baselines:
   - PC1/PC2/PC3 explain 44.9% / 27.7% / 19.3% of variance (91.9% total) and each maps to a cell-type
     axis (R^2 = 0.998-0.999 of each PC on cell line). The four types occupy separate quadrants with
     no sample-level overlap.
   - Silhouette score = 0.968 (scale -1 to 1); PERMANOVA R^2 = 0.999, p = 0.001.
   - Leave-one-out nearest-centroid classification: 573/573 = 100.0% accuracy.
   - Within-type replicate correlations (mean r = 0.962, min 0.863) do not overlap between-type
     correlations (mean r = 0.405, max 0.679).
   - Each type expresses its canonical lineage program: melanocytes MLANA/TYR/TYRP1/PMEL/SOX10
     (up to 12.7 log2FC vs other types); fibroblasts DCN/LUM/APOD/TNC; AoSMCs TAGLN/CNN1 plus a
     cytokine-rich baseline (IL1B/IL6/CXCL1/CXCL8); myoblasts DES/MYF5/ANKRD1/MGP.

2. Which cell types are most similar:
   - Centroid Pearson correlations (logCPM, 13,468 genes):
       Fibroblast - SkMyoblast  r = 0.891   <- MOST SIMILAR PAIR
       AoSMC      - SkMyoblast  r = 0.876
       AoSMC      - Fibroblast  r = 0.852
       Fibroblast - Melanocyte  r = 0.817
       Melanocyte - SkMyoblast  r = 0.818
       AoSMC      - Melanocyte  r = 0.803   <- most distant pair
   - Hierarchical clustering: fibroblasts and myoblasts merge first; AoSMCs join next; melanocytes
     are the outgroup. Biologically, the three mesoderm-derived mesenchymal/muscle cell types share a
     collagen/ECM-dominated program (e.g. COL1A1 logCPM 8.6-10.4 in all three), whereas neural-crest-
     derived melanocytes carry a unique pigmentation/neural program.

PRACTICAL IMPLICATION FOR COMPOUND PROFILING
Baseline identity is robust and cell-type-specific, so (i) any future sample that does not cluster with
its annotated cell type is a strong mislabeling/contamination QC alarm, and (ii) compound effects shared
across the three mesenchymal types should be interpreted as mesenchyme-shared rather than
cell-type-specific responses.

LIMITATION

Method (summary): For each of 24 BFA conditions (4 cell types x 6 doses), all 50 MSigDB
Hallmark gene sets were tested for suppression with a direction-aware competitive test
(one-sided Mann-Whitney U on DESeq2 Wald statistics, in-set vs background genes, BH FDR
across 1,200 tests), complemented by Fisher-exact enrichment among significantly
down-regulated genes (padj < 0.05). A pathway is "suppressed" when MWU q < 0.05 and the
median in-set log2 fold-change < 0. Full statistics: hallmark_geneset_direction_tests.csv,
hallmark_fisher_all_conditions.csv, hallmark_suppression_heatmap.png.

1) PATHWAYS SUPPRESSED IN ALL FOUR CELL TYPES (AoSMC, dermal fibroblast, melanocyte,
   skeletal muscle myoblast; significant in at least 5 of 6 doses per cell type unless noted):

   - Epithelial Mesenchymal Transition  (strongest; median gene-set log2FC at 300 nM =
     -1.44 / -1.45 / -1.57 / -0.89; ~80% of its genes individually padj<0.05-down;
     top down-enriched set in every cell type, Fisher q down to 1.3e-29)
   - TGF-beta Signaling
   - Angiogenesis
   - Apical Junction and Apical Surface
   - Coagulation
   - Complement
   - Inflammatory Response

   300 nM, q = 8.6e-17) and dermal fibroblasts.

2) SECRETORY-PATHWAY-PROXIMAL HALLMARK SETS ARE INDUCED, NOT SUPPRESSED:
   The two Hallmark sets that directly represent the secretory pathway - Unfolded Protein
   Response and Protein Secretion (plus mTORC1 Signaling and Myc Targets) - are
   significantly UP-regulated by BFA in every cell type (e.g., UPR median gene-set log2FC

   the expected on-target readout of a secretory-pathway disruptor: BFA blocks ER-to-Golgi

   UPR/secretory-adaptation program while REPRESSING the transcription of downstream
   secreted/membrane cargo programs.

   The pan-cell-type suppressed signature is dominated by Hallmark pathways whose protein
   products are secreted, ECM, or cell-surface molecules (EMT/collagens/MMPs, TGF-beta,

   cargo-producing programs - together with induction of the Unfolded Protein Response -
   is the coherent transcriptional footprint of secretory-pathway blockade: cells shut down
   synthesis of proteins that can no longer be trafficked. The signature is compound
   specific: Dexamethasone and Trichostatin A at matched doses show no EMT/cargo

Dabrafenib shows DIVERGENT, only partially consistent transcriptional responses across the four primary cell types.

Using the GDPx2 Drug-seq cohort (24 h treatment, 6 doses 9.5-3000 nM, ~28-32 replicate wells per condition after QC), I performed per-cell-type limma-voom differential expression of dabrafenib vs DMSO (21,478 genes; 878 QC-passed DMSO/dabrafenib samples) and compared the responses across human aortic smooth muscle cells (AoSMCs), dermal fibroblasts, melanocytes, and skeletal muscle myoblasts (SkMMs).

CONSISTENT (shared) component:
- All four cell types respond strongly and dose-dependently: from <=187 DEGs (FDR<0.05) at 9.5 nM up to 4,226 (AoSMC), 9,109 (fibroblast), 8,726 (melanocyte) and 6,306 (SkMM) DEGs at 3000 nM.
- A core of 884 genes (5.8% of the 15,236-gene union of DEGs at 3000 nM) is differentially expressed in all four cell types; 651 (73.6%) change in the same direction everywhere. This core is a shared integrated-stress/amino-acid-response program (up: SLC7A11, PSAT1, TRIB3, DDIT3/CHOP, ATF5, MTHFD2, tRNA synthetases) plus a shared anti-proliferative program (down: CDK1, CDC20, UBE2C, NUF2, RRM2; MKI67 down in all four, log2FC -0.96 to -2.53).

DIVERGENT component (dominant):
- Genome-wide log2FC correlations between cell types at 3000 nM are only weak to moderate (Spearman r = -0.05 to 0.41; mean 0.22). AoSMC and SkMM are the most concordant pair (r = 0.41; 94% of their 2,434 shared DEGs change in the same direction).
- Melanocytes are the clear outlier: their response is essentially uncorrelated with fibroblasts (r = -0.05) and SkMMs (r = 0.08), and among the 4,744 genes that are DEGs in both melanocytes and fibroblasts, 67% change in OPPOSITE directions.
- Mechanistically the sharpest divergence is the mevalonate/cholesterol-biosynthesis pathway (23 curated genes): coordinately REPRESSED in fibroblasts (mean log2FC -0.69; 21/23 significant, 0% up) and SkMMs (-0.34), but INDUCED in melanocytes (+0.29; 88% of significant genes up; e.g. HMGCS1 -1.28 in fibroblast vs +0.94 in melanocyte; INSIG1 -1.25 vs +0.70; LDLR -0.58 vs +0.70). Melanocytes also uniquely induce MYC (+0.47) and DUSP6, and carry 2,653 cell-type-exclusive DEGs (e.g. SEMA3E -3.1); fibroblasts have 2,224 exclusive DEGs (e.g. HES1 +2.1), SkMMs 1,026, AoSMCs 702.
- Dose-response shapes also differ: the AoSMC response peaks at 300-900 nM and partially contracts at 3000 nM (9,271 -> 4,226 DEGs), whereas fibroblast and melanocyte responses peak at 3000 nM, and melanocytes respond only weakly below 3000 nM (4 DEGs at 9.5 nM).

Interpretation for tissue-specific safety/efficacy: a common stress-response and cell-cycle-arrest axis (plausible basis for shared anti-proliferative effects and class toxicities of BRAF inhibitors in BRAF-wild-type tissue) is superimposed on much larger, cell-type-specific programs — including opposite-direction metabolic (cholesterol/lipid) rewiring in melanocytes versus fibroblasts/muscle cells. Consequently, transcriptional safety or efficacy readouts measured in one primary cell type cannot be assumed to extrapolate to the others; tissue-specific assessment is warranted.

Limitations: single 24-h timepoint; DMSO vehicle controls matched only at the lowest volume (0.0625%), so high-dose effects partially include vehicle; bulk 3' RNA-seq measures RNA, not protein/activity; donor variability unmodeled.
grader_notes: Agent performed a thorough limma-voom DE analysis with cross-cell-type comparisons and source-grounded interpretations, but failed to run the required ranked GSEA against MSigDB Hallmark pathways, so all pathway-specific criteria (3-6) are unmet; source reliability is strong.

SHARED GENETIC FACTORS AMONG NEONATAL METABOLITES (DA-24-3)

Analysis of discovery + replication GWAS summary statistics (20,474 SNPs x 13 metabolites) and the
per-sample abundance matrix (8,737 newborns x 75 metabolites) shows that the neonatal metabolome's
co-variation is driven by shared genetic factors at two levels:

1) SHARED (PLEIOTROPIC) LOCI
- CPT2 locus (chr1:75.7 Mb, 1p32.3): genome-wide significant for four traits at once - C6
  (P=2.9e-13), C8 (P=1.8e-10), C8/C2 (P=6.3e-10) and (C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 (P=1.2e-12), lead SNPs within
  ~10 kb. The same allele LOWERS medium-chain acylcarnitines C6/C8 and RAISES the diagnostic ratio
  (C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 (opposite-sign effects), mirroring their inverse phenotypic correlation (r~-0.4).
  CPT2 regenerates acyl-CoA from medium/long-chain acylcarnitines in mitochondria, so one variant
  plausibly shifts all these readouts together.
- chr5:50.1 Mb locus: shared by C6DC (P=4.6e-10) and C10:1 (P=9.6e-09), concordant positive effects
  on two desaturated medium/long-chain acylcarnitines of the same beta-oxidation pathway.

2) TRAIT-SPECIFIC LOCI MAP TO THE EXPECTED ENZYMES (internal validation of the architecture)
- C0 (free carnitine) -> chr11:68.6 Mb = CPT1A (P=3.6e-20)
- C4 (butyrylcarnitine) -> chr12:120.7 Mb = ACADS (P=5.4e-25)
- PRO (proline) -> chr22:18.9 Mb = PRODH (P=9.1e-42)
- TYR (tyrosine) -> chr12:121.9 Mb (HNF1A region, P=9.5e-34)
- C4DC+C5-OH -> chr9:129.1 Mb (P=1.3e-63); C8:1 -> chr16:20.5 Mb; C10:1 -> chr1:46.9 Mb
(11/13 lead loci replicated at P<0.05 same direction in the replication cohort; ORN/CIT has no
genome-wide significant locus.)

3) GENOME-WIDE GENETIC-EFFECT SHARING RECAPITULATES BIOCHEMISTRY
Correlation of per-SNP Z-scores (LD-thinned common SNPs, n=12,101) across trait pairs shows a
medium-chain acylcarnitine module with strong positive sharing: C6-C8 r=+0.78, C4-C6 +0.56,
C10:1-C8:1 +0.50, C10:1-C8 +0.47, C6DC-C8 +0.46, C8-C8/C2 +0.44; ratio traits inherit the sign of
their components ((C3DC+C4-OH)/C10 vs C8/C2: -0.40). Aromatic amino acids form a second, weaker
module (PRO-TYR +0.35). ORN/CIT is genetically isolated (|r|<=0.21 with all traits).

4) GENETIC SHARING EXPLAINS THE PHENOTYPIC SHARING
Across the 78 trait pairs, the genetic-effect correlation matrix and the phenotypic correlation
matrix (log1p abundances, 8,737 newborns) agree almost perfectly (Pearson r = 0.995,
P = 4.5e-78): e.g. C6-C8 +0.78 genetic vs +0.74 phenotypic. The observed co-variation of neonatal
metabolites is therefore dominated by shared genetic factors.

LIMITATIONS: loci are defined positionally (no rsID/LD panel), so the chr1:75.7 Mb and chr5:50.1 Mb
multi-trait signals are candidate (not formally colocalised) pleiotropic loci; Z-score correlation is
an effect-concordance proxy, not LDSC genetic correlation; 2 of 15 loci (C0 chr15, C6DC chr1:53 Mb)
did not replicate; only 13 of the ~75 metabolites were genome-scanned.
grader_notes: The analysis is strong for discovery/replication, locus definition, pleiotropic loci, and genetic-phenotypic correlation, but it omits fixed-effects meta-analysis and coloc.abf, resulting in low marks for those criteria.

FINAL ANSWER — DA-25-1
======================

1) TOP PATHOGENIC/ONCOGENIC MUTATED GENES IN TCGA-PRAD
------------------------------------------------------
The TCGA MAF (data_mutations_TCGA.txt; 40,731 mutation records across 499 tumors) contains no
ready-made pathogenicity column (the Hotspot and COSMIC annotation columns are empty), so
Pathogenic/Oncogenic alterations were defined operationally as:
  (A) truncating mutations (nonsense, frameshift indel, splice-site, nonstop, start-site)
      in genes with Cancer Gene Census evidence (annotated in the MAF) or in curated tumor
      suppressors (TP53, PTEN, APC, BRCA1/2, CDKN1B, SPOP, CHD1, ATM, KMT2C/D, ...), OR
  (B) missense / in-frame indels whose exact protein change recurs in >= 2 tumors
      (hotspot-recurrence signature of oncogenic selection).
This yields 1,379 Pathogenic/Oncogenic records covering 434/499 tumors (87%).

Top mutated genes (interpretable cancer-gene ranking, % of 499 tumors):
   1. SPOP    46 tumors (9.2%)  - recurrent hotspot missense (e.g. F133V); dominant driver
   2. TP53    40 tumors (8.0%)  - 19 truncating + recurrent missense
   3. CHEK2   21 tumors (4.2%)
   4. KMT2D   18 tumors (3.6%)  - nearly all truncating
   5. KMT2C   17 tumors (3.4%)  - nearly all truncating
   6. PTEN    11 tumors (2.2%)  - all truncating
   7. KDM6A    9 tumors (1.8%)
   8. APC      8 tumors (1.6%)
   9. NOTCH2   8 tumors (1.6%)
  10. CDK12 / CDKN1B / FIP1L1   6 tumors each (1.2%)
  then MED12, ARID2, CHD1, BRCA2, SETD2, PIK3CA (5 each), ATM, IDH1, NCOR1 (4 each).

Caveat: a naive frequency ranking of this legacy MAF is headed by FRG1B (16.4% of tumors),
followed by KRTAP4-11, RGPD8, NBPF10, UBBP4. These are sequencing/FFPE artifacts: their
"mutations" have median VAF ~5% (far below a clonal somatic variant) and recur at identical
residues across dozens of tumors. They must be excluded; the biologically meaningful top genes
are SPOP and TP53, matching the known TCGA primary prostate cancer driver landscape.

2) VISUALIZATION
----------------
Yes. Results were visualized with:
  - an oncoplot (gene x tumor matrix, top-20 Pathogenic/Oncogenic genes x 499 tumors, colored
    by alteration type, with per-gene cohort-frequency side bars):
      outputs/tcga_prad_pathogenic_oncoplot.png
  - a top-25 gene frequency bar chart (Cancer-Gene-Census/TSG genes highlighted) in the same file;
  - a T-stage association panel (per-gene mutation frequency by T stage, TP53 vs pathologic T
    stage, and a volcano plot of all 100 tested genes):
      outputs/tcga_prad_Tstage_association.png
Ranking tables are saved as outputs/top30_pathogenic_oncogenic_genes_*.csv.

3) GENE ASSOCIATION WITH CLINICAL T STAGE
-----------------------------------------
Method: 2x2 Fisher exact tests of mutated vs wild-type against binarized clinical T stage
(cT1-T2 organ-confined, n=351 vs cT3-T4 locally advanced, n=55; 94 patients lack clinical T
stage), for all genes mutated in >=5 (Pathogenic/Oncogenic set, 58 genes) or >=10 (all
non-synonymous set, 100 genes) patients, with Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction; plus an
ordinal Kendall-tau test across the full T-stage ordering and a sensitivity analysis against
pathologic T stage (pT2 n=188 vs pT3-T4 n=303).

Result: NO gene passes FDR correction against clinical T stage.
The leading, biologically coherent signal is TP53:
  - clinical T:   20.0% mutated in cT3-T4 vs 10.5% in cT1-T2 (OR=2.12, Fisher p=0.068)
  - ordinal test: Kendall tau=0.104, p=0.020
  - pathologic T: 16.2% mutated in pT3-T4 vs 5.9% in pT2 (OR=3.10, Fisher p=6.3e-4, FDR q=0.059)
TP53-mutant tumors are consistently enriched in locally advanced disease across all three
tests, with borderline FDR significance in the best-powered (pathologic T) analysis.
Weaker nominal signals: APC (p=0.035 vs clinical T, OR=6.7, q=1.0) and CHEK2 (p=0.08, OR=2.6).

Limitations: only 55 cT3-T4 patients (low power); clinical T stage is missing for ~19% of
patients and is noisier than pathologic staging; only SNVs/indels were tested - copy-number
losses (e.g. PTEN deletion) and fusions (TMPRSS2-ERG), major T-stage-relevant lesions in
prostate cancer, are not contained in this MAF.

Full methods, code, and intermediate counts are documented in trace.md.
grader_notes: The agent provides a solid, source-grounded analysis but diverges from the expected methodology and key reference results, particularly in the pathogenic filter definition, top gene ranking/frequencies, and FDR-significance of TP53 with pathologic T stage.
